On day 28 the difference was L246@P4: more than 5.0 logs and the number of Dpdx1 organisms L247@P4: dropped below the limit of detection. From day 42 L248@P4: onwards until the end of the experiment on day 84 neither L249@P4: Dpdx1 bacilli nor any revertants were observed. Additionally, the Dpdx1 mutant did not cause any visible gross L250@P4: pulmonary pathology nor was it capable of infecting the L251@P4: spleen (Fig. 4A and B). Genetic complementation L252@P4: restored virulence, demonstrating that the severe growth L253@P4: defect of Dpdx1 in mice was solely due to the disruption of L254@P4: the pdx1 gene. Our data show that bacterial de novo L255@P4: vitamin B6 biosynthesis is essential for survival and virulence of M. tuberculosis in the mouse model. L256@P4: Discussion L257@P4: We have demonstrated that M. tuberculosis synthesizes L258@P4: PLP via the ‘DXP-independent’ pathway by employing a L259@P4: synthase composed of Pdx1 and Pdx2 in line with L260@P4: reports from other species (Fig. 1) (Dong et al., 2004; L261@P4: Raschle et al., 2005; Tambasco-Studart et al., 2005; L262@P4: Gengenbacher et al., 2006; Knockel et al., 2007). Disruption of the pdx1 gene made the pathogen auxotrophic for L263@P4: vitamin B6. Furthermore, we could fully complement the L264@P4: phenotype in vitro by pdx1 under the control of its native L265@P4: promoter (Fig. 2A). This suggests that the downstream L266@P4: genes tesB2 and pdx2 in the knockout and complemented strain were expressed by the hygromycin promoter and thereby allowed formation of the PLP L267@P4: synthase by Pdx1 and Pdx2. L268@P4: Removal of exogenous vitamin B6 during exponential L269@P4: growth and aerated stationary phase resulted in the death L270@P4: of the bacillus, proving the essentiality of the PLP synthase in vitro (Fig. 2B and C). Hypoxic non-replicating L271@P4: cultures of wild-type M. tuberculosis overexpressed the L272@P4: PLP synthase. Surprisingly, Dpdx1 bacilli were impaired L273@P4: for regrowth upon oxygen exposure by direct plating on L274@P4: agar, but the loss of viability was prevented by re-aeration L275@P4: in liquid medium before cfu determination (Fig. 3B). Previous reports provided evidence that vitamin B6 can act L276@P4: as potent quencher of reactive oxygen species (Ehrenshaft et al., 1999; Jain and Lim, 2001; Matxain et al., L277@P4: 2009). Directly plated hypoxic non-replicating Dpdx1 L278@P4: bacilli probably have lost viability because of a lack of L279@P4: protection from oxygen radicals by vitamin B6. However, L280@P4: under aerated conditions wild-type organisms and the L281@P4: Dpdx1 mutant showed similar susceptibility to oxidative L282@P4: stress inducing agents (Fig. S2). An increased demand of L283@P4: PLP during dormancy is unlikely, as the major functions of L284@P4: vitamin B6 are related to amino acid metabolism and L285@P4: therefore to growth (Cole et al., 1998; Sassetti et al., L286@P4: 2003; Percudani and Peracchi, 2009). As a L306@P5: result of the multiple metabolic functions of vitamin B6 our L307@P5: results obtained from the Wayne model remain difficult L308@P5: to interpret and further experiments are required for L309@P5: clarification. L310@P5: Mycobacterium tuberculosis resides inside macrophages and extracellularly. Whether the intracellular bacillus L311@P5: can access host derived vitamin B6 and therefore would L312@P5: be resistant to inhibition of its PLP synthase is unclear. L313@P5: When we analysed the Dpdx1 mutant in a macrophage L314@P5: culture model, we did not observe any significant defect in L315@P5: survival compared with the wild-type or the complemented strain (Fig. S3). However, media required to maintain macrophages contained 4.9 mM pyridoxine, enough L316@P5: to allow optimal growth of M. tuberculosis in aerated cultures (Fig. 2A). Thus, the result might not reflect the L317@P5: situation in vivo. To gain further insights, we infected L318@P5: immunocompetent mice with the Dpdx1 mutant and L319@P5: observed a severe growth and survival defect, suggesting L320@P5: that vitamin B6 availability in the host is insufficient to L321@P5: support the pathogen in vivo (Fig. 4A). We did not observe L322@P5: secondary infection of the spleen, probably because of L323@P5: the clearance of Dpdx1 bacilli from the lungs, the primary L324@P5: site of infection (Fig. 4B). L325@P5: The most accurate estimation for overall vitamin B6 in L326@P5: the human body is the blood plasma concentration of PLP L327@P5: (Lui et al., 1985). Depending on nutritional and epidemiological influences, the presence of PLP in blood plasma of L328@P5: man fluctuates between 20 and 120 nM (Morris et al., L329@P5: 2008) or between 100 and 200 nM in mice (van de Kamp L330@P5: et al., 1995). However, the phosphorylated PLP molecule L331@P5: is expected to have a low permeability through biological L332@P5: membranes and thus cannot serve as vitamin B6 source L333@P5: for the Dpdx1 mutant in vitro (Fig. S4). The mouse blood L334@P5: plasma concentration of unphosphorylated and therefore L335@P5: membrane permeable B6 vitamers was reported to be L336@P5: < 800 nM. This concentration was insufficient to support L337@P5: optimal growth of the pathogen in vitro (Fig. 2A) (van de L338@P5: Kamp et al., 1995). The fact that we could not recover any L339@P5: bacilli from Dpdx1-infected mice beyond day 42 highlights L340@P5: the extraordinary sensitivity of the pathogen to vitamin B6 L341@P5: shortage. L342@P5: The Dpdx1 mutant has features essential for a successful vaccine candidate: it is attenuated by a non-reverting L343@P5: mutation and is avirulent, comparable to a strain deficient L344@P5: for the biosynthesis of vitamin B5 (Sambandamurthy L345@P5: et al., 2002). Our data warrant further investigation L346@P5: whether a pdx1 knockout could be exploited for vaccine L347@P5: development. In conclusion, the current study reveals the L348@P5: fundamental importance of vitamin B6 biosynthesis for L349@P5: survival and virulence of the tubercle bacillus and thus L350@P5: might offer an interesting pathway for the discovery of L351@P5: new antimycobacterials. L352@P5: Experimental procedures L353@P5: Strains and media L354@P5: Mycobacterium tuberculosis H37Rv (American Type Culture L355@P5: Collection #27294) was grown in Middlebrook 7H9 medium L356@P5: containing 0.2% glycerol, 0.5% BSA, 0.2% dextrose, 0.085% L357@P5: NaCl and 0.05% Tween-80, in Sauton’s minimal medium L358@P5: (0.5 g l-1 KH2PO4, 0.5 g l-1 MgSO4,2gl-1 citric acid, 0.05 g l-1 L359@P5: ferric ammonium citrate, 4 g l-1 asparagine, 6% glycerol, L360@P5: 0.05% Tween-80, pH 6.8), in Dubos medium containing 5 mM L361@P5: pyridoxine or on Middlebrook 7H11 agar supplemented with L362@P5: 10% oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase. Hypoxic nonreplicating bacilli were generated under slow stirring in sealed L363@P5: glass tubes as described previously (Lim et al., 1999). L364@P5: Cloning, expression and purification of Pdx1 and Pdx2 L365@P5: pdx1 (Rv2606c) and pdx2 (Rv2604c) were amplified from L366@P5: chromosomal DNA using specific primers (Table S1) and integrated into pET21a+ (Novagen). Both genes were expressed L367@P5: as C-terminal 6¥His–tag fusion proteins in BL21-CodonPlus L368@P5: (DE3)-RP (Stratagene). Upon induction with 0.1 mM and L369@P5: 0.4 mM isopropyl 1-thio-b-D-galactopyranoside, respectively, L370@P5: cells were grown in Terrific Broth medium for 20 h at 20°C L371@P5: (Pdx1) or for 5 h at 20°C (Pdx2). Bacteria were disrupted by L372@P5: sonication and the supernatant was cleared by centrifugation. L373@P5: Purification of the soluble His–tag proteins was carried out by L374@P5: Ni-NTA-agarose followed by size exclusion chromatography L375@P5: on a Superdex 200 10/300 GL column (GE Healthcare). The L376@P5: proteins were concentrated to 12 mg l-1 and stored at -80°C in L377@P5: 100 mM NaCl, 20 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, 10% glycerol. L378@P5: Enzyme assays L379@P5: The glutaminase activity of the equimolar Pdx1–Pdx2 L380@P5: complex was measured in a coupled enzyme assay in which L381@P5: the reduction of 3-acetylpyridine adenine dinucleotide L382@P5: (e= 8900 M-1 cm-1 L383@P5: ), an analogue of NAD+, was monitored at L384@P5: 363 nm (Gengenbacher et al., 2006). Glutamine concentrations varying from 0 to 15 mM produced typical Michaelis– L385@P5: Menten kinetics from which KM and kcat were calculated. The L386@P5: formation of PLP was analysed at 414 nm in 50 mM Tris-HCl L387@P5: pH 8 at 37°C containing 20 mM of the purified Pdx1 and/or L388@P5: Pdx2 and 1 mM of the substrates ribose 5-phosphate or L389@P5: ribulose 5-phosphate and dihydroxyacetone phosphate L390@P5: or DL-glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate (2 mM). Either 10 mM L391@P5: glutamine or 10 mM ammonium sulphate served as nitrogen L392@P5: source. The samples were pre-incubated for 30 min in the L393@P5: presence of all components except the C3 phosphosugar. L394@P5: Immunoblotting L395@P5: Lysates from M. tuberculosis in 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 8, L396@P5: 300 mM NaCl containing protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche) L397@P5: were prepared by beat beating and cleared by centrifugation L398@P5: at 14 000 g for 30 min at 4°C. Samples were separated on a L399@P5: NuPAGE 4–12% polyacrylamide gel (Invitrogen). Western L400@P5: blots were performed according to Kyhse-Andersen (KyhseAndersen, 1984). Pdx1 was detected by the cross reacting L401@P5: polyclonal AbPdx1 antibody, raised against the recombinant L402@P5: P. falciparum orthologue (53% sequence identity) at a L403@P5: Vitamin B6 biosynthesis of the tubercle bacillus 985 L404@P5-6: © 2010 Blackwell Publishing Ltd, Molecular Microbiology, 78, 980–9881:10 000 dilution (Gengenbacher et al., 2006). DHPS of M. L405@P6: tuberculosis was detected as described previously (Gengenbacher et al., 2008). Blots were developed using the L406@P6: enhanced chemiluminescence method. L407@P6: Gene knockout of pdx1 and complementation L408@P6: The pdx1 gene was interrupted by allelic exchange using the L409@P6: plasmid pYUB854 (Bardarov et al., 2002). Briefly, the flanking L410@P6: regions of the gene were amplified by PCR using specific L411@P6: oligonucleotides (Table S1) and inserted into pYUB854. M. L412@P6: tuberculosis was transformed using electroporation. We L413@P6: selected transformants with 80 mg ml-1 hygromycin B. The L414@P6: pdx1 mutant was complemented with the functional pdx1 L415@P6: gene using the integrative vector pMV306 (Stover et al., L416@P6: 1991). The gene including the putative promoter was amplified by PCR using specific oligonucleotides (Table S1) and L417@P6: inserted into pMV306. We transformed the pdx1 mutant by L418@P6: electroporation and selected transformants with 25 mg ml-1 L419@P6: kanamycin. Genomic DNA from hygromycin-resistant/ L420@P6: pyridoxine-requiring and complemented colonies was L421@P6: digested with KpnI/PvuII. The pdx1 gene deletion and L422@P6: complementation was confirmed by Southern blotting using L423@P6: the digoxigenin label and detection method (Roche). L424@P6: In vitro growth and survival studies L425@P6: Mycobacterium tuberculosis was maintained in Sauton’s L426@P6: medium supplemented with 5 mM pyridoxine. Cultures were L427@P6: pelleted and washed three times prior to dilution in fresh L428@P6: Sauton’s medium (OD600 0.05) without or with supplementation of pyridoxine at 0.05, 0.5, 5 and 50 mM concentrations. L429@P6: The OD600 was followed over time. To study survival under L430@P6: vitamin B6 deprivation, early log growing cultures were L431@P6: diluted in fresh Sauton’s medium/5 mM pyridoxine (OD600 L432@P6: 0.02) and incubated at 37°C/2 r.p.m. in 1 l roller bottles. L433@P6: During either exponential growth or the stationary phase, L434@P6: which were assessed by OD measurement, the cultures were L435@P6: pelleted, washed three times and resuspended in fresh Sauton’s medium. Survival over time was monitored by plating L436@P6: samples on 7H11 agar to estimate cfu. L437@P6: Cell uptake assay L438@P6: Exponentially growing bacilli were diluted in Dubos medium/ L439@P6: 5 mM pyridoxine to a final OD600 of 0.05 and transferred L440@P6: into a 24-well plate (1 ml per well). To each well 1 mCi L441@P6: of [3 L442@P6: H]-pyridoxine (20 Ci mmol-1, American Radiolabeled L443@P6: Chemicals) was added and incubated at 37°C. After 24 h L444@P6: plates were shifted into an anaerobic jar containing an L445@P6: oxygen absorbing gas pack (Oxoid). The removal of oxygen L446@P6: appeared over night and was monitored by decolorization L447@P6: of methylene blue. Bacilli were washed twice, resuspended L448@P6: in 50 ml 20% perchloric acid and inactivated by L449@P6: paraformaldehyde. Equal amounts of scintillation mix were L450@P6: added before counting. L451@P6: Mouse infection L452@P6: We infected 6- to 8-week-old female BALB/c mice (Biological L453@P6: Resource Centre) with early log phase M. tuberculosis L454@P6: H37Rv, Dpdx1 and Dpdx1comp cultures intranasally to deliver L455@P6: approximately 1000 cfu per animal. At different time points L456@P6: post infection lungs and spleen were removed and homogenized in PBS/0.05% Triton X-100. To quantify cfu, organ L457@P6: homogenates were plated on 7H11 agar supplemented with L458@P6: cycloheximide and ampicillin each at 10 mM. All procedures L459@P6: involving animals were reviewed and approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of the Novartis L460@P6: Institute for Tropical Diseases and were conducted according L461@P6: to national and international guidelines. To compare the L462@P6: viable cell counts recovered from the infected mice, one-way L463@P6: ANOVA with Tukey’s Multiple Comparison test was performed L464@P6: (Lenaerts et al., 2005). Statistical significance was accepted L465@P6: with P-values less than 0.001.
